question: Why did RUN-C Role-Agent not beat Factory Lite in TeamFlow?
implicationsForV05: v0.5 must use fewer roles (3-5) appropriate for large-project scale
v0.5 benchmark must use a genuinely large project (50+ features, 5+ independent modules)
True fork_context:false with owned scopes is non-negotiable
Overhead must be measured explicitly (agent count vs completion time vs quality)

overheadDominates.detail: Contract generation, scope enforcement, handoff verification, and agent lifecycle management added process overhead that outweighed parallelism benefits at TeamFlow scale.

noRealSpawnIsolation.detail: Early role-agent runs used fork_context:true or simulated roles. True fork_context:false isolation with owned scopes came later (DRY24).

projectTooSmall.detail: TeamFlow is a medium-scale project (~15-20 features). Multi-agent overhead (role coordination, contract generation, handoff verification) dominates at this scale. Benefit threshold likely requires 50+ features or 5+ independent modules.

tenRoleOverkill.detail: 10 roles (Founder/CTO/Architect/PM/Builder/Integrator/Verifier/Auditor/DevOps/Knowledge) for a medium project creates more coordination cost than division-of-labor benefit. 3-4 roles would be more appropriate for TeamFlow scale.

wrongComparison.detail: Comparing multi-agent to Factory Lite on a medium project is like comparing a factory assembly line to a craft workshop for making 5 chairs. The assembly line wins at 500 chairs.

insufficientParallelism.detail: TeamFlow modules were not independent enough for effective parallel agent work. Cross-module dependencies forced sequential integration regardless of agent count.

conclusion: RUN-C Role-Agent failure does NOT prove multi-agent is useless. It proves: (1) 10-role model was overkill for TeamFlow scale, (2) medium projects don't benefit from multi-agent overhead, (3) true fork_context:false isolation was not yet available. Multi-agent value for LARGE projects remains untested.
